title: Squeezed Chirp
hook: Catch the first black-hole merger ever heard.
sub: LIGO Night Shift: work the Livingston control room on 14 Sep 2015, set a squeezer dial across six real 18-qubit blur-core-v1 outputs (Atlas simulator) of the real GW150914 chirp, hit MERGER! at the peak and mark its pitch; each output's real measured blur caps the timing and pitch scores, the way LIGO's squeezed light trades one kind of quantum noise for another (an analogy, not a simulation).
you_control: Set: turn the squeezer dial across the five constant-product ratios and the isotropic control; each is a real engine output
Listen: START RUN counts 3-2-1, then plays that output's real audio while the spectrogram scrolls in, the lensed black holes merge on the real chirp and the end test masses swing with the real signal
Catch: hit MERGER! at the loudest moment, then drag the pitch line to the peak; tolerances are 2x the output's real measured widths, so no setting can max both scores
Explore: tap the numbered parts of three engraved plates (the Livingston site, the O1 interferometer, the quadruple pendulum), or open the data room to cut the real grids by hand
qubits_note: 257 x 257 grid padded by the engine to 512 x 512 = 9 + 9 qubits; engine status reports 'Recovered 18-qubit grid from measurement' for every job. 24 and 22 qubits were blocked by the API's 1 MiB request limit (413, measured); 20 qubits (640 x 640) ran but failed twice on Atlas's internal 2 MB result-payload limit (TMPRL1103). A 2-D grid cannot exceed 18 under these limits.
honesty: An analogy to squeezed light, not a simulation of it: blur-core-v1 ran on Atlas's classical statevector simulator, a classical Gaussian blur shows the same trade, the game scores are rules built from real measured widths (not a detection statistic), and the drawings are illustrations driven by the real signal.
